title: Signs of the Spirit who came as a dove
source_text: Πεπλήρωται δὲ ὁ νόμος καὶ οἱ προφῆται τῶν παραπλησίων παραδόξων τῷ ἀναγραφέντι περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ παρὰ τῷ βαπτίσματι περὶ τῆς περιστερᾶς καὶ τῆς ἐξ οὐρανοῦ φωνῆς. σημεῖον δὲ οἶμαι τοῦ τότε ὀφθέντος ἁγίου πνεύματος ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς τὰ ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ παράδοξα γεγενημένα, ἅτινα διαβάλλων Κέλσος φησὶν αὐτὸν παρ᾿ Αἰγυπτίοις μεμαθηκότα πεποιηκέναι. καὶ οὐκ ἐκείνοις γε μόνοις χρήσομαι ἀλλὰ γὰρ κατὰ τὸ εἰκὸς καὶ οἷς οἱ ἀπόστολοι τοῦ Ἰησοῦ πεποιήκασιν. οὐκ ἂν γὰρ χωρὶς δυνάμεων καὶ παραδόξων ἐκίνουν τοὺς καινῶν λόγων καὶ καινῶν μαθημάτων ἀκούοντας πρὸς τὸ καταλιπεῖν μὲν τὰ πάτρια παραδέξασθαι δὲ μετὰ κινδύνων τῶν μέχρι θανάτου τὰ τούτων μαθήματα. καὶ ἔτι ἴχνη τοῦ ἁγίου ἐκείνου πνεύματος, ὀφθέντος ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς, παρὰ Χριστιανοῖς σῴζεται. ἐξεπᾴδουσι δαίμονας καὶ πολλὰς ἰάσεις ἐπιτελοῦσι καὶ ὁρῶσί τινα κατὰ τὸ βούλημα τοῦ λόγου περὶ μελλόντων. κἂν χλευάσῃ δὲ Κέλσος τὸ λεχθησόμενον ἢ ὃν εἰσήγαγεν Ἰουδαῖον, ὅμως λελέξεται ὅτι πολλοὶ ὡσπερεὶ ἄκοντες προσεληλύθασι χριστιανισμῷ, πνεύματός τινος τρέψαντος αὐτῶν τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν αἰφνίδιον ἀπὸ τοῦ μισεῖν τὸν λόγον ἐπὶ τὸ ὑπεραποθανεῖν αὐτοῦ καὶ φαντασιώσαντος αὐτοὺς ὕπαρ ἢ ὄναρ. πολλὰ γὰρ καὶ τοιαῦτα ἱστορήσαμεν· ἅτινα ἐὰν γράφωμεν αὐτοὶ αὐτοῖς παρατυχόντες καὶ ἰδόντες. γέλωτα πλατὺν ὀφλήσομεν τοῖς ἀπίστοις, οἰομένοις ἡμᾶς ὁμοίως οἷς ὑπολαμβάνουσι ταῦτ᾿ ἀναπεπλακέναι καὶ αὐτοὺς πλάσσειν. ἀλλὰ γὰρ θεὸς μάρτυς τοῦ ἡμετέρου συνειδότος, βουλομένου οὐ διὰ ψευδῶν ἀπαγγελιῶν ἀλλὰ διά τινος ἐναργείας ποικίλης συνιστάνειν τὴν Ἰησοῦ θείαν διδασκαλίαν. ἐπεὶ δὲ Ἰουδαῖός ἐστιν ὁ περὶ τοῦ ἀναγεγραμμένου ἁγίου πνεύματος κατεληλυθέναι ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἀπορῶν, λεκτέον ἂν εἴη πρὸς αὐτόν· ὦ οὗτος, τίς ἐστιν ὁ ἐν τῷ Ἡσαΐᾳ λέγων· „καὶ νῦν κύριος ἀπέστειλέ με καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ;“ ἐν ῳ ἀμφιβόλου ὄντος τοῦ ῥητοῦ, πότερον ὁ πατὴρ καὶ τὸ ἄγιον πνεῦμα ἀπέστειλαν τὸν Ἰησοῦν, ἢ ὁ πατὴρ ἀπέστειλε τόν τε Χριστὸν καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, τὸ δεύτερόν ἐστιν ἀληθές. καὶ ἐπεὶ ἀπεστάλη ὁ σωτὴρ, εἶτα τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, ἵνα πληρωθῇ τὸ εἰρημένον ὑπὸ τοῦ προφήτου, ἐχρῆν δὲ τὴν τῆς προφητείας πλήρωσιν ἐγνῶσθαι καὶ τοῖς ἑξῆς· διὰ τοῦτο ἀνέγραψαν οἱ Ἰησοῦ μαθηταὶ τὸ γεγενημένον.
pass_a_gloss: The law and the prophets have been filled (πληρόω) with marvels (παράδοξα) closely like (παραπλήσιος) the thing recorded about Jesus at the baptism (βάπτισμα), about the dove (περιστερά) and the voice (φωνή) from heaven. And as a sign (σημεῖον), I think (οἶμαι), of the Holy Spirit (ἅγιον πνεῦμα) then seen in the form of a dove (ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς) [are] the marvels done by Jesus, which Celsus, slandering (διαβάλλω), says he did having learned among Egyptians. And I will use not those alone but, as is likely/fitting (κατὰ τὸ εἰκός), also those which the apostles (ἀπόστολοι) of Jesus did. For without powers (δυνάμεις) and marvels they would not have moved (κινέω) those hearing new words (καινοὶ λόγοι) and new teachings (μαθήματα) to abandon (καταλείπω) ancestral things (τὰ πάτρια) and to accept, with dangers (κίνδυνοι) up to death, the teachings of these men. And still traces (ἴχνη) of that Holy Spirit, seen in dove-form, are preserved (σῴζω) among Christians. They charm away / exorcise (ἐξεπᾴδω) demons (δαίμονες) and accomplish many healings (ἰάσεις) and see certain things about future things according to the will (βούλημα) of the Word/reason (λόγος). Even if Celsus mocks (χλευάζω) what will be said, or the Jew he introduced (εἰσάγω), nevertheless it will be said that many as it were unwilling (ἄκοντες) have come to Christianity (χριστιανισμός), some spirit having turned (τρέπω) their ruling part (ἡγεμονικόν) suddenly (αἰφνίδιον) from hating the word/message (λόγος) to dying on its behalf (ὑπεραποθνῄσκω), and having presented visions (φαντασιόω) to them awake or in dream (ὕπαρ ἢ ὄναρ). For we have learned/known (ἱστορέω) many such things; which if we write, we ourselves having been present (παρατυγχάνω) and having seen, we shall incur (ὀφλισκάνω) broad laughter (γέλως πλατύς) from the unbelieving (ἄπιστοι), who think that we, like those whom they suppose to have fabricated (ἀναπλάσσω) these things, also ourselves fabricate (πλάσσω). But God is witness (μάρτυς) of our conscience (συνειδός), wishing to commend (συνίστημι) not through false reports (ψευδεῖς ἀπαγγελίαι) but through a manifold clear evidence (ἐνάργεια ποικίλη) the divine teaching (θεία διδασκαλία) of Jesus. And since it is a Jew who is at a loss (ἀπορέω) about the Holy Spirit recorded to have come down in dove-form upon Jesus, it should be said to him: 'O you, who is it in Isaiah saying, "And now the Lord (κύριος) sent me (ἀποστέλλω), and his Spirit"?' In which, the phrase (ῥητόν) being ambiguous (ἀμφίβολος), whether the Father (πατήρ) and the Holy Spirit sent Jesus, or the Father sent both Christ and the Holy Spirit, the second is true. And since the Saviour (σωτήρ) was sent, then the Holy Spirit, in order that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled, and the fulfilment (πλήρωσις) of the prophecy had to be known also to those after, therefore the disciples of Jesus recorded what had happened.
pass_b_english: The law and the prophets are full of marvels like the one recorded about Jesus at his baptism, concerning the dove and the voice from heaven (Matthew 3:16–17; Mark 1:10–11; Luke 3:21–22). And I think that the marvels Jesus performed are a sign that the Holy Spirit was then seen in the form of a dove; Celsus slanders these, saying that he learned them among the Egyptians and so performed them. I will appeal not to those alone but also, as is reasonable, to the ones the apostles of Jesus performed. For without mighty works and marvels they would not have moved those who heard new doctrines and new teachings to leave their ancestral ways and to accept these men's teachings at the risk even of death. And traces of that Holy Spirit who was seen in the form of a dove are still preserved among Christians. They drive out demons, perform many healings, and, as the Word wills, see certain things about the future.

Celsus may mock what I am about to say, or the Jew he has brought in may, but it shall be said all the same: many have come to Christianity as if against their will. Some spirit suddenly turned their ruling mind from hating the message to dying for it, and showed them visions, waking or in dreams. For we have learned of many such things; and if we, who were present ourselves and saw them, were to write them down, we would draw loud laughter from unbelievers, who think that we too, like those they suppose to have made up these things, are making them up. But God is witness to our conscience, which wishes to commend the divine teaching of Jesus not by false reports but by clear evidence of many kinds.

But since it is a Jew who raises difficulties about the Holy Spirit, recorded to have come down upon Jesus in the form of a dove, we should say to him: Sir, who is it that says in Isaiah, “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah 48:16)? Since the phrase there is ambiguous, whether the Father and the Holy Spirit sent Jesus, or the Father sent both Christ and the Holy Spirit, the second is true. And since the Saviour was sent, and then the Holy Spirit, so that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled, and the fulfilment of the prophecy had to be made known to those who came after as well, for this reason the disciples of Jesus recorded what took place.

choices.choice: κατὰ τὸ βούλημα τοῦ λόγου taken as 'as the Word wills' (Christ the Logos, capitalised); 'as reason wills' is grammatically possible but less likely in Origen. τὸν λόγον in 'from hating the λόγος' is the Christian message, so lowercase 'the message'. ἐξεπᾴδουσι literally 'charm away (by incantation)'; rendered 'drive out' since Origen means Christian exorcism, not spells. The staged text has a full stop after ἰδόντες; read as a comma (the ἐάν clause runs into ὀφλήσομεν). βουλομένου read as agreeing with συνειδότος (our conscience). 'God is witness' is a Pauline formula (Romans 1:9; 1 Thessalonians 2:5); possible echo only, not cited inline. Isaiah 48:16: LXX and English numbering agree; Origen's text lacks 'GOD' after 'Lord' (as LXX). The fulfilment formula ('so that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled') is Matthew's stock phrase, not one verse; uncited. 'In the form of a dove' (εἴδει) is Luke 3:22's wording, covered by the first citation. Reviewer: ἅτινα ἐὰν γράφωμεν αὐτοὶ αὐτοῖς παρατυχόντες καὶ ἰδόντες is not restrictive ('only the ones we saw'); the participles describe the writers as eyewitnesses. λεκτέον ἂν εἴη keeps its sense of obligation ('we should say').
κατὰ τὸ εἰκός: 'as is fitting' -> 'as is reasonable'
natural order for κινδύνων τῶν μέχρι θανάτου: 'at the risk even of death'
ἅτινα ... παρατυχόντες καὶ ἰδόντες: removed restrictive 'the ones we were present at' and the added 'Yet'; 'have known' -> 'have learned of'
'evidence plain and manifold' -> 'clear evidence of many kinds'
λεκτέον ἂν εἴη: 'one might say' -> 'we should say' (obligation kept)
